The alphabet: twenty-four letters.back: gáma — a soft voiced *gh*; a *y* sound before ε and ι
kápa — says *k*, with no puff of air
lámda — says a light *l*, never the dark English one
ni — says *n*. Looks like a Latin v.
pi — says *p*, with no puff of air
ro — one tapped *r*, as in Spanish *pero*
sígma — says *s*; ς only at the end of a word
taf — says *t*, with no puff of air
khi — the *ch* of Scottish *loch*; lighter before ε and ι
psi — says *ps*, including at the start of a word
ōméga — says *o* as in lot, exactly like ο

The five vowel sounds, and the many ways.back: a, e, i, o, u — no length, no reduction, no glides
ι, η, υ, ει, οι, υι
The five vowel sounds, and the many ways.extra: Which one a word takes is a fact about that word.

The five vowel sounds, and the many ways.back: ου — the only way. There is no single letter for it.

The vowel digraphs: αι ει οι ου υι.extra: Unmarked, the pair is one sound.

The consonant digraphs: μπ ντ γκ γγ.front: Why Greek has no letter for b, d or g
The consonant digraphs: μπ ντ γκ γγ.back: β δ γ softened to *v*, *th* and *gh* in antiquity, and the stops are written μπ, ντ, γκ instead

The stress accent: what it marks, and wh.back: Which syllable is stressed — nothing else. One per word, compulsory from two syllables up.

The stress accent: what it marks, and wh.back: All-capital text takes none; a single initial capital keeps its accent — **Άννα**, but **ΑΘΗΝΑ**

Where the stress falls: the last three s.back: The stress is always on one of the last three syllables — never the fourth from the end
